lessons.title: Pay attention to your body language

blocks.text: Dogs as masters of observation
Our dog recognises the smallest gestures and body reactions and acts on these insights consistently.
Dogs interpret gestures, movements and even mood on the basis of pace, muscle tone and facial expression.
It is essential to behave towards the dog in a harmonious, calm and composed manner.
Subtle signals directly influence the dog's behaviour, sense of security and trust.

Our dog observes us very attentively. It recognises the smallest gestures and body reactions. It acts on these insights consistently. Dogs are extremely sensitive in their grasp of the body language of their human companion. They interpret gestures, movements and even mood on the basis of factors such as pace, muscle tone, speed of movement, gait and facial expression.
Signals and their effect
Gestures: calm, clear and deliberate gestures signal reliability and security to the dog. Abrupt or hectic gestures, on the other hand, can convey uncertainty or threat.
Movements: gentle, flowing movements have a calming effect, while jerky or uncoordinated movements can make the dog nervous or put it on alert.
Mood: dogs sense the emotional state of their human. A balanced, positive mood promotes relaxation in the dog, while tension or anger is transferred to it.
Pace: a moderate, even pace in interaction shows control and composure. A pace that is too fast or irregular can be perceived as stress or impatience.
Muscle tone: relaxed muscle tone radiates calm. Tension or a stiff body signals strain, which can unsettle the dog.
Gait: a confident, relaxed gait conveys authority. A rushed or uncertain gait can raise doubts in the dog about the human's role as leader.
Facial expression: a friendly, relaxed facial expression has a calming effect. A tense or angry look can frighten the dog or put it in a defensive mood.

lessons.title: Body language from a professional perspective

blocks.text: What dogs recognise in humans

Dogs understand human pointing gestures. In experiments (Hare et al., 2002), dogs found hidden targets when a human pointed at them or looked at them. They did this better than wolves raised by humans.

Dogs follow a human's gaze especially when the human has previously spoken to them directly or looked at them (Téglás et al., 2012). Eye contact and address announce to the dog that a signal is coming.

Dogs perceive movements very well. They recognise details at greater distances less well than humans. At a distance, large, clear movements are therefore effective, while small gestures are more easily overlooked.
First establish attention, then give the signal
First establish eye contact or briefly speak to your dog. Only then give the signal.
Use one unambiguous signal for each behaviour and always use it in the same way. Changing gestures and words for the same behaviour make learning harder for the dog.
Make sure that posture, voice and gesture express the same thing. Contradictory signals, for example a friendly voice with a tense posture, unsettle the dog.
Hold a signal only as long as is necessary for the behaviour. End it clearly and then move calmly again.
Posture during approach and encounters
Approaching head-on, bending over the dog and staring directly are experienced by dogs in unclear situations as intrusive or threatening.
Approach a dog rather in a slight arc, preferably not directly, and with an inner open and friendly attitude.
Direct your gaze softly into the surroundings in the direction of the dog. Do not focus on the dog.
Stroke the dog calmly with flowing movements.
Individual experiences and breed influence how a dog reacts to an approach. Therefore always observe its reaction and adapt your behaviour.
Exercise: filming your own body language
Have yourself filmed for two to three minutes during a training session or a walk with your dog.
Watch the video without sound. Pay attention to walking speed, shoulder tension, arm movements, direction of gaze and posture of the upper body.
In the same scene, observe your dog: when does it orient itself towards you, when does it seem unsettled or distracted?
Note your observations under “My reflection” at the end of this page and decide on one point that you will change deliberately in the coming week.

Sources: Hare B., Brown M., Williamson C., Tomasello M. (2002): The domestication of social cognition in dogs. Science 298 (5598), 1634–1636. Téglás E., Gergely A., Kupán K., Miklósi Á., Topál J. (2012): Dogs' gaze following is tuned to human communicative signals. Current Biology 22 (3), 209–212.
Practice impulse: calm through slowing down

In your activities with the dog, carry out your interactions deliberately calmly and slowly. Pay attention to relaxed muscle tone and a calm voice. Observe how much more attentively and calmly your dog reacts to this “quiet” body language.
Positive consequences of observing this

When the human observes these principles, a trusting bond develops between them and their dog. The dog feels safe and orients itself towards the calm leadership of its owner. In the social environment, for example when meeting strangers, other dogs or animals in nature, the dog stays composed and balanced. It reacts less fearfully or aggressively, because it judges the situation as non-threatening through its human's body language. This makes walks, social interactions and living together as a whole easier. The dog is also perceived as well trained, which strengthens the owner's reputation.
Negative consequences of not observing this

If the human ignores these insights and appears restless, hectic or tense, this is transferred to the dog. An insecure or stressed dog can bark excessively, back away or even snap when meeting people. Towards other dogs it can react aggressively or fearfully, which leads to conflicts. In nature it could rush impulsively at wild animals or panic, which is dangerous both for it and for the environment. In the long term this can strain the relationship with the dog, undermine its trust and reinforce behaviour problems such as hyperactivity or anxiety.

The human's harmonious, calm and composed body language is the basis for a stable relationship with the dog. It acts like a mirror in which the dog orients itself, and decisively shapes its behaviour, whether in urban everyday life, in the social environment or in nature. Anyone who takes these principles to heart promotes not only the well-being and leadability of their dog, but also peaceful coexistence with the social environment. If these insights are neglected, one risks misunderstandings, stress, poor leadability and problematic situations.
